title: Only rational numbers have repetitive digit sequences

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Only rational numbers have repetitive digit sequences

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Every rational number p/q has a digit sequence that eventually repeats (with period at most q - 1), and rational numbers are the only numbers with repetitive digit sequences.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In fact, rational numbers turn out to be the only kinds of numbers that have repetitive digit sequences.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 4, “Systems Based on Numbers”; section “Mathematical Constants” (from p. 136), p. 141. Scope: digit expansions of real numbers

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch04-14: resolvable-now, resolvability 1.00

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: This is a standard checkable theorem with an elementary proof in any fixed integer base. The proof directly covers the full scope and cleanly distinguishes rational from irrational numbers.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Use the standard theorem that a real number has an eventually periodic positional expansion in an integer base if and only if it is rational. Long division gives eventual period at most q minus one for p/q after reduction, subject to the usual terminating-expansion convention.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: Terminating expansions have an alternative representation ending in repeating maximal digits.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 1.0
analysis feasibility: 1.0
data existence: 1.0
discriminating power: 1.0
data adequacy: 1.0

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Both directions are elementary and published: long division has finitely many remainders, so every rational eventually repeats with period at most q-1, and an eventually periodic expansion is a finite geometric series, hence rational. The argument covers every integer base and every real, which is the claim's scope. Checking published periods of 1/q is only a sanity check on top of the proof.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: A real number has an eventually periodic digit expansion in an integer base if and only if it is rational, and for p/q the repeating block has length at most q-1 because the division remainder is an integer in 1, ..., q-1. A non-rational with an eventually periodic expansion, or a rational p/q whose minimal period exceeds q-1, would refute the claim; the standard remainder argument rules both out.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: Terminating expansions are eventually periodic with repeating 0, and the statement has to be read that way or terminating rationals look like counterexamples.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.95
operationalizability: 0.95
data existence: 0.85
discriminating power: 0.95
analysis feasibility: 0.9

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: In any integer base, every rational p/q has an eventually periodic digit expansion with period at most q - 1 (and preperiod + period at most q), every eventually periodic digit sequence is the expansion of a rational number, and the published digit expansions of irrational constants show no eventual periodicity.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py (1) runs long division for 1/q, q = 1..20000, and for all p/q with q <= 300, in bases 2, 3 and 10 (64,850 expansions per base), recording preperiod and period from the first repeated remainder and counting violations of period <= q-1 or preperiod + period <= q; base-10 periods of 1/n are compared with the 10,000-term OEIS A007732 b-file. (2) It draws 20,000 random eventually periodic patterns (base in {2,3,10}, preperiod 0-20 digits, block 1-30 digits, all-(b-1) blocks rejected), reconstructs the exact rational with Python Fractions and re-expands it, counting patterns not reproduced digit for digit. (3) It downloads the first 10,000 decimal digits of sqrt(2), e and pi from OEIS and, for every p <= N/3, finds the smallest index after which the digit sequence agrees with its shift by p, flagging any p for which two full periods already agree. Run time about 9 s including downloads.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: (1) for bases 2, 3 and 10 and all denominators q = 1..20000, the digit expansion of 1/q (and of p/q for all 1 <= p < q when q <= 300) has period <= q - 1 and preperiod + period <= q, with zero violations, and the base-10 periods of 1/q agree with OEIS A007732 for every n covered by its b-file; (2) 100% of 20000 random eventually periodic digit patterns (random preperiod of length 0..20, random non-trivial period block of length 1..30, bases 2, 3, 10) are reproduced exactly when the rational number reconstructed from them is re-expanded by long division; (3) none of the first 10000 decimal digits of sqrt(2), e and pi (OEIS b-files) is eventually periodic in the sense that, for some period p <= N/3, the last 2p digits already repeat with period p.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered: any rational whose expansion has minimal period > q - 1 or does not become periodic within q digits; any disagreement with A007732; any eventually periodic pattern whose reconstructed rational re-expands differently; or an irrational constant's published digits exhibiting at least two full agreeing periods for some p <= N/3.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: rational expansions violating period <= q-1 or preperiod + period <= q (out of 194,550)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Wolfram's 'repetitive digit sequences' are eventually periodic positional expansions in an integer base; the clause 'period at most q - 1' in the claim text is the standard long-division bound (there are only q - 1 non-zero remainders). Terminating expansions are treated as eventually periodic with repeating 0, as the assessors note; period blocks consisting only of the digit b - 1 are excluded from the random patterns because they denote the alternative expansion of a terminating rational and would re-expand in the terminating form. The converse ('rationals are the only numbers with repetitive digit sequences') is tested constructively (every eventually periodic pattern reconstructs to a rational that reproduces it) and, as a sanity check only, on the published digits of three irrational constants; a finite digit string can never prove non-periodicity, so part (3) is a consistency check rather than a proof.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Preperiod and period of 1/q (q <= 20000) and p/q (q <= 300) in bases 2, 3, 10 by long division (generated by analysis.py)

OEIS A007732: period of decimal representation of 1/n, b-file

20000 random eventually periodic digit patterns (numpy default_rng seed 20261031; generated by analysis.py)

OEIS A002193: decimal expansion of sqrt(2), b-file

OEIS A001113: decimal expansion of e, b-file

OEIS A000796: decimal expansion of pi, b-file

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Both directions are classical theorems; the computation confirms the forward direction exhaustively for all denominators up to 20,000 in three bases (the bound period = q - 1 is attained, e.g. for full-reptend primes), agrees with OEIS A007732 on all 10,000 tabulated decimal periods, and confirms the converse constructively on 20,000 random eventually periodic patterns.

A finite digit string cannot establish that a number is not eventually periodic; part (3) only checks that 10,000 published digits of sqrt(2), e and pi show no two agreeing repeats for any period up to N/3 (the maximal agreement found was 1.33 periods, consistent with chance), which is a consistency check, not a proof of the 'only rationals' clause.

Terminating expansions are counted as eventually periodic with repeating 0 (period 1), following OEIS A007732; under the alternative convention (repeating b-1) they are still eventually periodic, so the verdict does not depend on this choice.
